dufflepud.example: But they soon got it mixed up with their old name of Duffers and finally settled down to calling themselves the Dufflepuds; and that is what they will probably be called for centuries.
examples: But they soon got it mixed up with their old name of Duffers and finally settled down to calling themselves the Dufflepuds; and that is what they will probably be called for centuries.

paragraphs.context: THERE WAS A BOY CALLED EUSTACE CLARENCE Scrubb, and he almost deserved it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace Clarence Scrubb is a boy with modern parents. He calls them Harold and Alberta, and their house has very little furniture.
paragraphs.simple: There was a boy called Eustace Clarence Scrubb. He almost deserved the name. His parents called him Eustace Clarence, and his teachers called him Scrubb. I cannot tell you what his friends called him, because he had none. He did not call his father and mother ‘Father’ and ‘Mother’. He called them Harold and Alberta. They were very up-to-date and advanced people. They ate no meat, did not smoke and did not drink. They also wore a special kind of underclothes. In their house there was very little furniture and very few clothes on the beds. The windows were always open.

paragraphs.context: Last year, when he had been staying with the Pevensies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace likes to tease the Pevensies about Narnia. He thinks they make it all up.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Still playing your old game?’ said Eustace Clarence. He had been listening outside the door, and now he came into the room with a big smile. Last year he had stayed with the Pevensies. Then he had managed to hear them all talk about Narnia, and he loved to tease them about it. He thought, of course, that they were making it all up. He was far too stupid to make up anything himself, so he did not like that.

paragraphs.context: I swore an oath that, if once I established peace in Narnia
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the day he became king, Caspian made a promise. He said he would sail east for a year and a day to find his father’s friends, or to learn how they died.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Well, on the day I became king, Aslan agreed. I made a promise. I said that if I could make peace in Narnia, I would sail east myself for a year and a day. I would find my father’s friends, or I would learn that they were dead. And if I could, I would punish the men who killed them. These were their names: the Lord Revilian, the Lord Bern, the Lord Argoz, the Lord Mavramorn, the Lord Octesian, the Lord Restimar, and—oh, that other one who is so hard to remember.’

paragraphs.context: hardly had they raised their cups to their lips
paragraphs.mainIdea: Caspian and his friends sit down with a new man. Then his men catch all five visitors very fast.
paragraphs.simple: Caspian thanked the man. But neither he nor the others much liked the look of their new friend. All of them sat down. They had hardly raised their cups to their lips when the black-haired man nodded to his men. Then, as quick as lightning, strong arms were round all five of the visitors. They fought for a moment, but the other side had all the advantages. Soon everyone had no weapons and had their hands tied behind their backs. Only Reepicheep was still fighting. A man held him tight, and he moved about and bit the man hard.

paragraphs.context: they plucked Gumpas out of his chair and deposited him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bern and Drinian throw the Governor’s table to one side. They take Gumpas out of his chair, and Caspian sits in it.
paragraphs.simple: Caspian nodded to Bern and then stood to one side. Bern and Drinian took a step forward. Each took one end of the table. They lifted it and threw it to one side of the hall. It rolled over, and letters, papers, ink-pots, pens and sealing-wax flew everywhere. Then they took Gumpas out of his chair. They were not rough, but they held him as firmly as if their hands were steel. They put him down about four feet away, facing the chair. Caspian sat down in the chair at once. He laid his bare sword across his knees.

paragraphs.context: He began, almost for the first time in his life, to feel lonely
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace begins to feel lonely and afraid. He thinks the others may have left him behind on purpose.
paragraphs.simple: But Eustace did not enjoy himself, or not for very long. For almost the first time in his life, he began to feel lonely. At first this feeling grew very slowly. Then he began to worry about the time. There was not the slightest sound. Suddenly he thought that he might have been lying there for hours. Perhaps the others had gone! Perhaps they had let him walk away on purpose, just so they could leave him behind! He jumped up in a panic and started to go down.

paragraphs.context: It reached the pool and slid its horrible scaly chin down over the gravel
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dragon reaches the pool, but it dies before it can drink.
paragraphs.simple: The dragon reached the pool. It put its ugly chin, which was covered in scales, down on the small stones to drink. But before it drank, it made a great croaking or clanging cry. After a few twitches it rolled onto its side. It lay quite still with one claw in the air. A little dark blood ran out of its wide-open mouth. The smoke from its nose turned black for a moment and then floated away. No more came.

paragraphs.context: the bracelet which he had shoved up above his elbow had become strangely tight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace wakes with a pain in his arm. The bracelet on his arm has become strangely tight, and his arm must have swollen.
paragraphs.simple: Eustace slept and slept. What woke him was a pain in his arm. The moon was shining into the mouth of the cave. The bed of treasure seemed to have become much more comfortable. In fact he could hardly feel it at all. At first he did not know why his arm hurt. But after a while he thought of the bracelet that he had pushed up above his elbow. It had become strangely tight. His arm must have swollen while he was asleep. It was his left arm.

paragraphs.context: it only means I had another smaller suit on underneath the first one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace tells how he took off a skin. His feet were still scaly, so he thought he had another skin under it. He took that off too and went to wash.
paragraphs.simple: ‘But just as I was going to put my feet into the water, I looked down. I saw that they were all hard and rough and wrinkled and scaly, just as they had been before. Oh, that is all right, said I. It only means I had another smaller suit on under the first one. I will have to get out of it too. So I scratched and tore again, and this underskin peeled off well. I stepped out and left it lying next to the other one. Then I went down to the well for my bathe.’

paragraphs.context: Great was the rejoicing when Edmund and the restored Eustace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everyone is glad when Eustace comes back as a boy. They hear his story and do not want to go back for the gold.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone was very happy when Edmund and the boy Eustace walked into the breakfast circle round the camp fire. Now, of course, everyone heard the earlier part of his story. People wondered if the other dragon had killed the Lord Octesian several years ago. Or maybe Octesian himself had been the old dragon. The jewels that Eustace had filled his pockets with in the cave were gone. So were the clothes he had been wearing. No one wanted to go back to that valley for more treasure, and Eustace wanted it least of all.

paragraphs.context: Still it stretched and stretched till its head was over the starboard bulwark
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Sea Serpent does not jump at the ship. It puts its head over the ship and down into the water, so the whole ship is under the arch of its body.
paragraphs.simple: But the Sea Serpent did not jump at them. It shot its head forward across the ship, level with the yard of the mast. Now its head was just next to the fighting-top. Still it stretched and stretched, until its head was over the starboard side. Then it began to come down, not onto the crowded deck but into the water. So the whole ship was under an arch made by the Serpent. Almost at once the arch began to get smaller. On the starboard side the Sea Serpent was now almost touching the side of the Dawn Treader.

paragraphs.context: on the bottom lay a life-size figure of a man, made apparently of gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the bottom of a clear pool there is a figure that seems to be made of gold. When the sun comes out, Lucy thinks it is the most beautiful statue she has seen.
paragraphs.simple: The bottom of the pool was made of large grayish-blue stones. The water was very clear. On the bottom lay the figure of a man, as big as a real man. It seemed to be made of gold. It lay face down with its arms stretched out above its head. Just as they looked at it, the clouds opened and the sun shone out. The golden shape was lit up from one end to the other. Lucy thought it was the most beautiful statue she had ever seen.

paragraphs.context: It is folly to think of avoiding an invisible enemy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says it is silly to try to keep away from an enemy that no one can see. He wants to meet the enemy face to face.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Your Majesties all,’ said Reepicheep, ‘hear me. It is silly to think we can keep away from an enemy that we cannot see, however much we creep and hide. If these creatures want to bring us to battle, they will do it. And whatever comes of it, I would rather meet them face to face than be caught by the tail.’

paragraphs.context: her fingers tingled when she touched it as if it were full of electricity
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy touches the book on the desk, and her fingers tingle. It is shut with two lead clasps, and it opens easily when she undoes them.
paragraphs.simple: She went up to the desk and put her hand on the book. Her fingers tingled when she touched it, as if it were full of electricity. She tried to open it, but at first she could not. This was only because it was shut with two lead clasps. When she had undone them, it opened easily. And what a book it was!

paragraphs.context: I knew when I let the Duffers make themselves invisible
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Magician says he knew that Lucy would come to take the spell off the Duffers. He was not sure of the day, and being invisible makes him sleepy.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Well, of course I knew, when I let the Duffers make themselves invisible, that you would come soon to take the spell off. I was not quite sure of the exact day. And I was not especially watching this morning. You see, they had made me invisible too. Being invisible always makes me so sleepy. Heigh-ho—there, I am yawning again. Are you hungry?’

paragraphs.context: If by use you mean filling our bellies or our purses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says the Dark Island may be of no use, but they came for honor and adventure. To turn back would hurt the honor of them all.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Use?’ said Reepicheep. ‘Use, Captain? If you mean filling our stomachs or our bags of money, I agree that it will be of no use at all. As far as I know, we did not sail to look for useful things. We came to look for honor and adventure. And here is as great an adventure as any I have ever heard of. If we turn back here, it hurts all our honor a great deal.’

paragraphs.context: we have had a lot of queer adventures on this voyage of ours
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund is not sure that it is safe to eat the food or to trust the girl. Strange things have happened on their voyage, and things are not always what they seem.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Look here,’ he said. ‘I hope I am not a coward, I mean about eating this food. And I am sure I do not want to be rude. But we have had a lot of strange adventures on this voyage of ours, and things are not always what they seem. When I look in your face, I cannot help believing all you say. But that is just what might happen with a witch too. How are we to know you are a friend?’

paragraphs.context: no wonder, for the days when I was a star had ceased long before
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Old Man says that his name is Ramandu. He was once a star, long before the men on the ship knew this world.
paragraphs.simple: ‘I was a long way above the air, my son,’ said the Old Man. ‘I am Ramandu. But I see that you stare at one another. You have not heard this name. And that is no wonder. The days when I was a star ended long before any of you knew this world. And all the groups of stars in the sky have changed.’

paragraphs.context: When she sinks, I shall swim east with my four paws
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says he will go east as long as he can. He will use the ship, then his small boat, and then he will swim.
paragraphs.simple: ‘No. Why should Your Majesty expect it?’ said Reepicheep, in a voice that most people heard. ‘My own plans are made. While I can, I sail east in the Dawn Treader. When she fails me, I paddle east in my small boat. When she sinks, I will swim east with my four paws. And when I can swim no longer, I will sink with my nose to the sunrise. This is if I have not reached Aslan’s country, or gone over the edge of the world in some great waterfall. Then Peepiceek will be the head of the talking mice in Narnia.’

paragraphs.context: here at last the sky did really come down and join the earth
paragraphs.mainIdea: As they go on, the sky looks like a blue wall that joins the earth. It looks more like glass than anything else.
paragraphs.simple: In a flat place with no trees, the sky always looks as if it comes down to meet the grass in front of you. But as they went on, they got a very strange feeling. Here, at last, the sky really did come down and join the earth. It was a blue wall, very bright, but real and hard. It looked more like glass than anything else. Soon they were quite sure of it. It was very near now.

paragraphs.context: I am opening the door in the sky
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan opens the door in the sky. In one moment, the children are back in their own world.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Child,’ said Aslan, ‘do you really need to know that? Come, I am opening the door in the sky.’ Then, all in one moment, the blue wall tore open, like a curtain being torn. A terrible white light came from beyond the sky. They felt Aslan’s mane and a Lion’s kiss on their foreheads. And then they were in the back bedroom in Aunt Alberta’s home in Cambridge.

sentences.context: Last year, when he had been staying with the Pevensies
sentences.simple: Last year he stayed with the Pevensies. At that time he managed to hear them all talk about Narnia, and he loved to tease them about it.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been staying’ (past perfect continuous) is a stay that was already in the past before the story’s ‘now’; ‘when’ tells the time.

sentences.context: she couldn’t get rid of it because it had been a wedding present
sentences.simple: Aunt Alberta did not like the picture. But she could not get rid of it, because someone she did not want to upset had given it to her when she was married.
sentences.grammar: ‘it had been a wedding present’ is past perfect: it gives the reason, which came before ‘she couldn’t get rid of it’.

sentences.context: At the same moment an exercise book which had been lying beside Edmund
sentences.simple: At the same moment, a school book that had been lying next to Edmund on the bed moved. It rose and flew across the room to the wall behind him. Lucy felt her hair whipping round her face.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been lying’ is a relative clause in the past perfect continuous: the book was lying there before it rose.

sentences.context: which Narnia had owned when Lucy and Edmund had reigned there
sentences.simple: The Dawn Treader was small next to the big ships that Narnia had owned when Lucy and Edmund ruled there.
sentences.grammar: ‘which Narnia had owned’ is a relative clause about the ships; ‘had owned’ and ‘had reigned’ are past perfect because that time was before the voyage.

sentences.context: Why exactly Eustace had slipped and reeled and stumbled all the way forward
sentences.simple: I never heard why Eustace had slipped and stumbled all the way to the front of the ship. He did not yet walk well on a ship.
sentences.grammar: The ‘Why exactly ...’ clause is the object of ‘heard’ and is put first; inside it the word order is normal (‘Eustace had slipped’), not a question.

sentences.context: if once I established peace in Narnia, I would sail east myself
sentences.simple: On the day he became king, Caspian made a promise. He said that when there was peace in Narnia, he would sail east for a year and a day to find his father’s friends.
sentences.grammar: ‘would sail’ is ‘will sail’ seen from the past: it says what he promised then; ‘if once I established peace’ means ‘as soon as I had made peace’.

sentences.context: Oars were used only when wind failed or for getting in
sentences.simple: People used the oars only when there was no wind, or to take the ship in and out of the harbor.
sentences.grammar: ‘Oars were used’ is passive: it tells what was done to the oars, not who used them; ‘for getting in’ is ‘for’ plus an -ing word.

sentences.context: If Caspian had been as experienced then as he became later on
sentences.simple: Caspian was not as experienced then as he later became. If he had been, he would not have made this suggestion. But at that time it seemed a very good one.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + verb’ talks about something that did not happen: he was not experienced, so he made the mistake.

sentences.context: But hardly had they raised their cups to their lips
sentences.simple: They had only just lifted their cups to their lips when the black-haired man nodded to his men.
sentences.grammar: ‘hardly had they raised’ is inversion: after ‘hardly’ at the start, ‘had’ comes before ‘they’; it means ‘they had just raised ... when’ the next thing happened.

sentences.context: where they found many other unfortunate prisoners; for Pug was of course a pirate
sentences.simple: They were taken to a long, rather dark place on the slave-ship. There they found many other unlucky prisoners, because Pug was a pirate.
sentences.grammar: ‘where they found ...’ is a clause about the place; ‘for’ here means ‘because’ and gives the reason.

sentences.context: and wondered what was happening to Caspian and tried to stop Eustace talking
sentences.simple: They sat in the straw. They wondered what was happening to Caspian. They tried to stop Eustace from talking as if everyone but him was wrong.
sentences.grammar: ‘was happening’ is the past continuous for something going on at that time; ‘what ...’ is an indirect question, so the word order is normal; ‘stop Eustace talking’ is ‘stop + person + -ing’.

sentences.context: At first, the only people who cheered were those who had been warned
sentences.simple: At first the only people who cheered were the ones that Bern’s messenger had told. They knew what was happening, and they wanted it to happen.
sentences.grammar: ‘those who had been warned’ is a ‘who’ clause in the passive past perfect: they were warned earlier, by someone else.

sentences.context: Had he known that Caspian had only one ship and one ship’s company
sentences.simple: If he had known that Caspian had only one ship and its crew, he would have spoken softly for the moment.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had he known’ means ‘If he had known’ (inversion, no ‘if’); it talks about something that was not true.

sentences.context: Bern could only tell them that he had seen his six companions sail away
sentences.simple: If Gumpas had known that Caspian had only one ship and its crew, he would have spoken softly for the moment.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had he known’ means ‘If he had known’ (inversion, no ‘if’); it is about the past and about something that was not true.

sentences.context: the old Eustace, Harold and Alberta’s Eustace, would have given up the climb
sentences.simple: The old Eustace would have stopped climbing after about ten minutes. But this Eustace did not.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have given up’ says what the old Eustace would have done; it did not happen, because he was now different.

sentences.context: Perhaps they had let him wander away on purpose simply
sentences.simple: Maybe the others had let him walk away on purpose, just so they could leave him behind.
sentences.grammar: ‘Perhaps they had let’ uses the past perfect for a guess about something earlier; ‘in order to’ gives the aim.

sentences.context: The dragon-that-had-been-Eustace held out its sore leg gladly enough
sentences.simple: The dragon that had once been Eustace held out its sore leg, and was glad enough to do it. It remembered how Lucy’s cordial had cured him of seasickness before he became a dragon.
sentences.grammar: ‘dragon-that-had-been-Eustace’ is a whole phrase joined with hyphens to work like one name; ‘had been’ and ‘had cured’ are past perfect for things before that time.

sentences.context: Eustace (unlike most boys) had never thought much of treasure
sentences.simple: Unlike most boys, Eustace had never cared much about treasure. But now he saw at once how useful it would be in this new world, which he had walked into by mistake through the picture.
sentences.grammar: ‘had never thought much of’ (past perfect) means that before then he had not valued treasure; the brackets (unlike most boys) add a small extra remark.

sentences.context: that one which was dead at about three o’clock that afternoon
sentences.simple: They tried to feel better. Everyone told everyone else that there were not likely to be more dragons. The dragon they saw was dead at about three o’clock that afternoon. So it could hardly have been killing people only a few hours before.
sentences.grammar: ‘would hardly have been killing’: ‘would have + past participle’ is a guess about the past, and ‘hardly’ makes it very unlikely that it was killing people hours before.

sentences.context: The bracelet which had fitted very nicely on the upper arm of a boy
sentences.simple: The bracelet had fitted well on a boy’s arm. It was much too small for the thick leg of a dragon.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had fitted’ is a ‘which’ clause in the past perfect; it tells us how the bracelet was before Eustace changed.

sentences.context: since the first day he came on board he had been an unmitigated nuisance
sentences.simple: Eustace saw more and more clearly that he had been a big trouble to everyone since his first day on the ship. He saw that now he was even more trouble.
sentences.grammar: ‘he had been’ (past perfect) looks back from the moment he understood; ‘since’ marks the starting time.

sentences.context: He was a very humane killer too, for he could dispatch a beast
sentences.simple: He was also a kind killer. He could kill an animal with one blow of his tail, so that it did not know it had been killed.
sentences.grammar: ‘so that it didn’t know’ gives the result; ‘it had been killed’ is a passive past perfect: the killing was already done.

sentences.context: instead of pursuing the ship it turned its head round
sentences.simple: The animal was very stupid. It did not follow the ship. It turned its head and sniffed along its own body, as if it hoped to find the Dawn Treader there.
sentences.grammar: ‘instead of + -ing’ means ‘not doing X, but doing Y’; ‘as if it expected’ tells what the animal seemed to think.

sentences.context: If it had been a hot day, no doubt some would have been tempted
sentences.simple: It was not a hot day. If it had been hot, some of them would have wanted to swim, and everyone would have had a drink.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + had been ..., would have been tempted’ (passive) is about a past that was not real: it was not a hot day.

sentences.context: we wouldn’t let them go away alive unless they’d done the needful for us
sentences.simple: We would not let the strangers go away alive, unless they had done what we needed.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘they’d done’ is the past perfect (‘they had done’) for something that must be finished first.

sentences.context: more than one doubted whether Lucy had not merely imagined
sentences.simple: When they saw the boat and the empty sand, more than one of them wondered if Lucy had only imagined everything she told them.
sentences.grammar: ‘doubted whether Lucy had not merely imagined’: the ‘not’ does not make it negative; it means they thought she might have only imagined it. ‘all she had told them’ has no ‘that’.

sentences.context: she remembered what she had been told about the Magician walking
sentences.simple: She remembered what people had told her about the Magician. He walked on bare feet and made no more noise than a cat.
sentences.grammar: ‘what she had been told’ is a passive past perfect noun clause: it means ‘the things that someone had told her’.

sentences.context: where she felt quite sure there had been no picture before
sentences.simple: In the middle of the writing, where she felt quite sure there had been no picture before, she saw the great face of Aslan. He was staring into hers.
sentences.grammar: ‘where’ starts a clause about the place; ‘there had been no picture’ (past perfect) compares it with earlier.

sentences.context: Of course I could turn him into something else, or even put a spell
sentences.simple: Of course I could turn him into something else. Or I could put a spell on him so that they would not believe a word he said.
sentences.grammar: ‘could’ says what was possible; ‘a spell ... which would make them not believe’ is a relative clause about the spell, and ‘would make’ is its result.

sentences.context: which were so widely opened that he seemed to have no eyelids at all
sentences.simple: You noticed his eyes most. They were so wide open that he seemed to have no eyelids. He stared as if he was in terrible fear.
sentences.grammar: ‘so ... that ...’ shows a result; ‘which’ adds more information about his eyes.

sentences.context: there was set out such a banquet as had never been seen
sentences.simple: On the table there was a great feast. No one had ever seen such a feast, not even when Peter the High King kept his court at Cair Paravel.
sentences.grammar: ‘such a banquet as had never been seen’: ‘such ... as’ means ‘of the kind that’; ‘had never been seen’ is a passive past perfect, so it compares with every feast before.

sentences.context: while they had been talking the stars had grown fainter
sentences.simple: They could see it better now. While they were talking, the stars had become fainter, and big gaps of white light were opening in the east.
sentences.grammar: ‘while they had been talking’ (past perfect continuous) is the time before they saw the sky; ‘had grown fainter’ is the change that happened during it.

sentences.context: whether the sun at its rising did not look bigger in these seas
sentences.simple: Once or twice before, the Narnians had wondered if the sun looked bigger in these seas than it had at home.
sentences.grammar: ‘wondered whether ...’ starts an indirect question; ‘did not look bigger’ here just means ‘looked bigger’; ‘than it had looked’ (past perfect) compares with earlier times at home.

sentences.context: They could not have seen even the sun if their eyes
sentences.simple: They could not have looked even at the sun if the water of the Last Sea had not made their eyes strong.
sentences.grammar: ‘could not have seen ... if ... had not been strengthened’ (passive) is about the past: the water did make their eyes strong.

sentences.context: and if their eyes had not by now grown as strong as eagles’
sentences.simple: This last sea looked very like the Arctic. If their eyes had not become as strong as an eagle’s, the sun on all that white would have been too bright to bear.
sentences.grammar: ‘if ... had not grown, ... would have been unbearable’ is a past ‘if’ sentence: their eyes did grow strong, so it was not too bright.

sentences.context: back in our own world everyone soon started saying how Eustace had improved
sentences.simple: Back in our own world, everyone soon said that Eustace had got better. Only Aunt Alberta said he had become ordinary and annoying.
sentences.grammar: ‘how Eustace had improved’ is a noun clause with the past perfect: the change came before the people spoke.

get rid of.meaning: To throw away something or make it go away.
get rid of.example: she couldn’t get rid of it because it had been a wedding present

make up.meaning: To invent a story that is not true.
make up.example: they were making it all up

put up with.meaning: To accept something bad and not complain.
put up with.example: The others can put up with it if they like

shut up.meaning: To make someone stop talking, or to stop talking. It can be rude.
shut up.example: if we don’t shut him up

make do with.meaning: To use what you have when there is nothing better.
make do with.example: You’ll have to make do with some of mine.

burst into tears.example: Lucy burst into tears and Edmund looked very blank

turn out.meaning: To be, in the end, a certain thing, when you did not know before.
turn out.example: It turned out to be the remains of a mailshirt.

get on with.meaning: To go on with something, or to start it.
get on with.example: Well,” said Caspian at last, “let’s get on with it.

give in.meaning: To stop fighting or arguing, and do what the other side wants.
give in.example: it was such obvious sense that they had to give in

stand by.example: Stand by to heave him up, men,” said Caspian.

sooner or later.meaning: At some time in the future, but you do not know when.
sooner or later.example: we’d have to go back to our own world sooner or later

hold on to.example: Hold on to my hand, Caspian, while I lean out over the water a bit.”

come true.example: This is the island where dreams come true.”

look out.meaning: To be careful; to watch for danger.
look out.example: Edmund, who knew something about magic, sprang after him, warning him to look out and not to be a fool.

keep on.example: as his mouth kept on getting filled with water

take off.meaning: To remove clothes, or to end a spell.
take off.example: Take off his shirt, Tacks, and let the gentlemen see

give way.meaning: To let something else come first.
give way.example: even a question of honor must give way

make for.example: rode out into the town and made for the slave market.

go on.meaning: To continue, or to say more after a stop.
go on.example: and went on, “Where are my friends?”

all at once.meaning: At the same time, or very suddenly.
all at once.example: the number of things he thought of saying all at once nearly suffocated him

in the end.meaning: After a long time or much trouble; at last.
